lead: Electricity harms the body in proportion to the current that flows through it, not the voltage printed on the casing. Skin resistance turns a voltage into a current through V = I R. A tingle through dry skin and a fatal shock through wet skin can come from the same socket. The same rule explains why a few tens of microamps pushed straight into the heart by a catheter can be more dangerous than a hundred times that current through intact skin. These two cases are called macro-shock and micro-shock, and hospital electrical design is built around the second.
prereq: You need first-year circuit ideas, V = I R and series and parallel resistances, and the electrode-to-skin behaviour from electrode theory.

sections.h3: The body as a resistor: current does the damage

blocks.text: A person becomes part of a circuit when two points of the body touch a live conductor and a return path. The current through the body follows Ohm's law. The damage depends on that current, its path and how long it flows; the voltage on the casing only sets how much current the resistance will pass.

Skin is the main resistor. Dry, intact skin gives about 10 kΩ hand to hand; wet or broken skin gives about 1 kΩ or less. Inside the body the resistance falls to a few hundred ohms, roughly 300 Ω to 500 Ω. Contact area, calluses and sweat all move these numbers.

blocks.where: I is the body current in amperes, V is the touch voltage in volts, and R is the resistance of the current path in ohms. For milliamps, I(mA) = 1000 × V / R.

blocks.text: Path matters because current density matters. A hand-to-hand or hand-to-foot path crosses the heart; a finger-to-finger path mostly does not. The same current squeezed through a small contact point heats tissue and causes a burn.

items: Dry skin, hand to hand: about 10 kΩ.
Wet skin, hand to hand: about 1 kΩ.
Internal path from a catheter: a few hundred ohms, with no skin in the way.

sections.h3: The effects ladder at mains frequency

blocks.text: At 50 Hz or 60 Hz the effects rise in a fixed order as current increases. The values below are for a current path through the trunk and a shock lasting about one second.

items: 1 mA: faint tingle, the perception level.
10 mA to 15 mA: let-go level. The hand grips the conductor and cannot release it, because the flexor muscles are stronger than the extensors.
20 mA to 30 mA: respiratory tetanus. The chest muscles clamp and breathing stops while the current flows.
About 100 mA: ventricular fibrillation, the usual cause of death in an electric shock.
Several amperes: deep burns and cardiac arrest; the heart may be clamped rather than fibrillating.

blocks.text: Why is 50/60 Hz the worst frequency? Nerve and muscle membranes are most easily driven by alternating currents in the tens of hertz. At direct current, or at radio frequencies, a much larger current is needed for the same excitation. Mains frequency sits in that worst band.

Duration changes the outcome. A 100 mA shock for a second is dangerous; the same current for a few milliseconds may not fibrillate. Short contacts still burn, because heating goes as I²R at the contact point.

Macro-shock means current enters through intact skin. Skin resistance limits the current, so the source must be tens or hundreds of volts to push a dangerous current. The ICU example below is a macro-shock calculation.

Micro-shock means an insulated conductor, a saline-filled catheter or a pacing lead carries current directly to the heart. Skin resistance is absent. About 100 µA, and in some studies as little as 20 µA, can fibrillate the heart. The 10 µA patient-leakage limit applies to type CF parts, the ones allowed to touch the heart, and leaves a safety margin; type B and BF parts, which touch only intact skin, may leak up to 100 µA.

Micro-shock also depends on timing. The heart is most vulnerable during the T wave, the repolarisation phase, roughly the last third of each beat. A small pulse landing in that window can start fibrillation; the same pulse outside the window often cannot.
That is why an intracardiac lead needs its own protection: isolation, current-limiting resistors and careful earthing. The three defences and the four tests are in Electrical safety and testing.

examples.question: A patient in an ICU touches the metal casing of a faulty monitor at 230 V. (a) The hand-to-hand path through dry skin is 10 kΩ. (b) The same path through wet skin is 1 kΩ. (c) Later, a saline-filled catheter gives a 500 Ω path to the heart, and a 0.1 V offset appears across it. Find the body current in each case and compare it with the 100 mA fibrillation level and the 10 µA patient-leakage limit for cardiac-connected (type CF) equipment.
steps: 23 mA is above the 10–15 mA let-go level and below the 100 mA fibrillation level. The shock is painful and may freeze the muscles, but it usually does not fibrillate the heart.
230 mA is 2.3 times the 100 mA fibrillation level, so a shock lasting about a second is likely to fibrillate.

200 µA is twenty times the 10 µA limit for cardiac-connected equipment and above the roughly 100 µA that can fibrillate the heart directly, so it is a micro-shock hazard even though the voltage is only 0.1 V.
examples.answer: 23 mA through dry skin, 230 mA through wet skin, and 200 µA through the catheter; the wet-skin and catheter cases exceed their danger levels.

traps: Saying high voltage is dangerous and stopping there. A 230 V source is harmless through 100 kΩ and lethal through 1 kΩ; the current decides.

Writing micro-shock limits in milliamps. The intracardiac danger level is tens to about a hundred microamps, a thousand to several thousand times smaller than the 100 mA macro-shock level (20 µA is 5000 times smaller).
Mixing up let-go and fibrillation. Let-go is 10–15 mA; fibrillation is near 100 mA for a one-second shock.
Ignoring duration and timing. A short pulse, or a pulse outside the T wave, is far less likely to fibrillate than a one-second shock.
Treating body resistance as one fixed number. It changes tenfold between dry and wet skin and drops again once a conductor is inside the body.

quiz.q: State the approximate current levels for perception, let-go and ventricular fibrillation at mains frequency.
quiz.a: About 1 mA for perception, 10–15 mA for let-go, and about 100 mA for ventricular fibrillation in a shock of about one second.

quiz.q: Why is 50 Hz alternating current more dangerous than the same current at DC?
quiz.a: Nerve and muscle membranes are excited most easily by alternating current in the tens of hertz. DC needs a much larger current to produce the same effect, so mains frequency lies in the worst band.

quiz.q: A faulty monitor puts 120 V across a wet hand-to-hand path of 2 kΩ. Find the current. Is it above the let-go level?
quiz.a: I = V / R = 120 / 2000 = 0.06 A = 60 mA. This is well above the 10–15 mA let-go level and below the 100 mA fibrillation level.

quiz.q: A catheter gives a 500 Ω path to the heart, and 0.05 V appears across it. Find the current in microamps.
quiz.a: I = 0.05 / 500 = 0.0001 A = 100 µA. This is ten times the 10 µA type CF limit and in the range that can fibrillate the heart.

quiz.q: Explain why the leakage limit for an intracardiac connection is set in microamps while the fibrillation level for macro-shock is around 100 mA.
quiz.a: In a macro-shock the skin and tissue resistance limit the current, and the current spreads over the whole trunk. In a micro-shock the conductor delivers current directly to a small patch of heart muscle, so the current density needed to disturb the heart is reached at a much smaller current.

quiz.q: Why does the T wave matter in micro-shock, and what design change follows from it?
quiz.a: During the T wave much of the ventricle is repolarising and is vulnerable, so a small current can start fibrillation. Design follows: limit leakage to 10 µA (type CF), isolate patient connections, and keep current paths away from the heart.

beyond: Not for the exam. Standards such as IEC 60601-1 turn these ideas into measurable leakage and isolation limits for every medical device. Hospital biomedical departments use a safety analyser to measure earth continuity, insulation resistance and leakage current on each device before it touches a patient. Research on the vulnerable period of the heart shapes defibrillator timing and the design of implantable leads. Search next for patient leakage current, microshock, and current-time danger zones.
